Each question is worth one mark, and there are seventy-five minutes for twenty of them — three minutes
and forty-five seconds each. Almost every question on this paper can also be done the long way, and the
long way takes six or seven minutes. So the paper is not really asking whether you can do the
mathematics. It is asking whether you can find the short route.

## Question 1

::: {.topic}
Topic — completing the square; the vertex form of a quadratic
:::

::: {.question}
$\mathrm f(x)$ is a quadratic function in $x$. The graph of $y = \mathrm f(x)$ passes through the point
$(1, -1)$ and has a turning point at $(-1, 3)$. Find an expression for $\mathrm f(x)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-x^2-2x+2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-x^2+2x+3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $x^2-2x$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $x^2+2x-4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $2x^2+4x+1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $-2x^2-4x+5$
:::

To pin down a quadratic you need two things: [a point the curve passes through]{.hl}, and [the turning
point]{.hl}. The turning point is the more useful of the two, because it is [the place where the
parabola folds back on itself]{.hl} — so it tells you about the shape, not just the position. This
question hands you both, so use both.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

We are told the turning point, so [let's start from the vertex form]{.hl}

$$\mathrm f(x) = a(x-h)^2 + k , \qquad \text{where the turning point is } (h,k) .$$

Here $(h,k) = (-1,3)$, so

$$\mathrm f(x) = a(x+1)^2 + 3 .$$

That uses up one of the two facts, and we have one unknown left — the number $a$ out at the front. So
[the other fact should be just enough to finish the job]{.hl}. The curve goes through $(1,-1)$, so
[substitute $x=1$ and $\mathrm f(x) = -1$]{.hl}:

$$-1 = a(1+1)^2 + 3 = 4a + 3 , \qquad \text{so} \qquad 4a = -4 \qquad \text{and} \qquad a = -1 .$$

Before we expand, check the sign makes sense. We got $a = -1$, and [a negative $a$ means the parabola
opens downwards]{.hl} — which it has to, because the curve turns at a height of $3$ and later comes down
to $-1$. So [the turning point is a maximum]{.hl}, and the picture agrees with the algebra.

Now just expand:

$$\mathrm f(x) = -(x+1)^2 + 3 = -x^2 - 2x + 2 ,$$

which is **option A**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **B** | $-(x-1)^2+4$ — this turns at $(1,4)$. A sign slip: $(x-1)$ was written when the turning point is at $x=-1$. |
| **C** | $(x-1)^2-1$ — this turns at $(1,-1)$. The two given facts have been swapped, using the point *on* the curve as the turning point. |
| **D** | $(x+1)^2-5$ — goes through $(1,-1)$, but turns at $(-1,-5)$. Here $a=1$ was assumed instead of worked out. |
| **E** | $2(x+1)^2-1$ — right $x$ for the vertex, wrong $y$: the $-1$ has been taken from the other point. |
| **F** | $-2(x+1)^2+7$ — goes through $(1,-1)$, but $a$ is wrong. |

Watch out for D and F. They really do go through $(1,-1)$, so if you check your answer by substituting
that point, you will happily confirm a wrong option. [Checking one condition is not checking]{.hl} — a
quadratic needs both facts.
:::

## Question 2

::: {.topic}
Topic — the discriminant as a condition; quadratic inequalities
:::

::: {.question}
Find the complete set of values of the real constant $k$ for which the expression
$$x^2 + kx + 2x + 1 - 2k$$
is positive for all real values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-12<k<0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $k<-12$ or $k>0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $-\sqrt6-3<k<\sqrt6-3$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $k<-\sqrt6-3$ or $k>\sqrt6-3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $-2<k<\tfrac12$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $k<-2$ or $k>\tfrac12$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** $0<k<4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $k<0$ or $k>4$
:::

*Positive for all real values of $x$* is really a statement about the graph. The coefficient of $x^2$ is
positive, so [the parabola opens upwards]{.hl}; if it is to stay above the axis everywhere, then [it
must never cross the $x$-axis]{.hl}. In other words [it has no real roots, so the discriminant is
negative]{.hl}.

Two things to watch. The coefficient of $x$ is $k+2$, not $k$ — the $x$ terms have been split up on
purpose. And what you end up with is *another* quadratic inequality, this time in $k$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

First [collect like terms]{.hl}:

$$x^2 + (k+2)x + (1-2k) .$$

So $a = 1$, $b = k+2$, $c = 1-2k$.

For the expression to be positive everywhere, we need no real roots, so we need [the discriminant to be
less than zero]{.hl}. It has to be *strictly* less than zero: if it were equal to zero the parabola
would [just touch the $x$-axis]{.hl}, and at that point the expression would equal zero — and zero is
not positive.

$$b^2 - 4ac = (k+2)^2 - 4(1-2k) = k^2 + 4k + 4 - 4 + 8k = k^2 + 12k < 0 .$$

Factorising,

$$k(k+12) < 0 .$$

Now be careful, because this is a quadratic in $k$ and you cannot just read the answer off. Sketch it:
it is a parabola in $k$, opening upwards, crossing at $k=0$ and $k=-12$. [The curve is below the axis
between the roots]{.hl}, so

$$-12 < k < 0 ,$$

which is **option A**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **B** | The other way round — $k(k+12)<0$ has been read as true *outside* the roots. This is the classic mistake with quadratic inequalities, and it is exactly why you sketch. |
| **G** | Used $c = 1+2k$ instead of $1-2k$. That gives $k^2 - 4k < 0$, so $0<k<4$. One sign. |
| **H** | The same sign slip, plus the same "outside the roots" mistake as B. |
| **E**, **F** | Made out of the numbers $-2$ and $12$, which both appear in the working — in $k+2$, and in $k^2+12k$ — but neither of which is a root. |
| **C**, **D** | The roots of $k^2+6k+3=0$. No natural slip gives these; they are just decoys. |
:::

## Question 3

::: {.topic}
Topic — binomial coefficients; the sum of the first $n$ integers
:::

::: {.question}
Find the coefficient of $x$ in the expression
$$(1+x)^0 + (1+x)^1 + (1+x)^2 + (1+x)^3 + \cdots + (1+x)^{79} + (1+x)^{80} .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $80$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $81$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $324$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $628$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $3240$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $3321$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $6480$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $6642$
:::

Eighty-one brackets looks like a lot of work, but [we only want the coefficient of $x$]{.hl}, so we can
ignore every other term. And [the coefficient of $x$ in $(1+x)^n$ is just $n$]{.hl} — to get an $x$ term
you [pick the $x$ from exactly one bracket]{.hl} and a $1$ from all the others, and there are $n$
brackets you could pick it from. So the whole thing turns into a sum you already know.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The coefficient of $x$ in $(1+x)^n$ is $\dbinom{n}{1} = n$. So we just [add up the $n$ values]{.hl} from
each bracket:

$$0 + 1 + 2 + \cdots + 80 = \frac{80 \times 81}{2} = 3240 ,$$

which is **option E**. $\blacksquare$

Notice that [we never expanded anything]{.hl}. All the work was in spotting which single term could
contribute, and then recognising the sum that was left.

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** | $80$ — only the last bracket's contribution. |
| **B** | $81$ — counted *how many* brackets there are, instead of adding them. |
| **G** | $6480 = 80 \times 81$ — forgot to divide by 2. |
| **F** | $3321 = 3240 + 81$ — one bracket too many. |
| **H** | $6642 = 2 \times 3321$ — both slips together. |
| **C**, **D** | $324$ and $628$ — no clear origin. |
:::

## Question 4

::: {.topic}
Topic — recurrence relations; laws of indices
:::

::: {.question}
The sequence $x_n$ is given by $x_1 = 10$ and $x_{n+1} = \sqrt{x_n}$ for $n \ge 1$. What is the value of
$x_{100}$? *(Here $a^{b^c}$ means $a^{(b^c)}$.)*

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $10^{2^{99}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $10^{2^{100}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $10^{2^{-99}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $10^{2^{-100}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $10^{-2^{99}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $10^{-2^{100}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** $10^{-2^{-99}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $10^{-2^{-100}}$
:::

[Have a look at the options before you start.]{.hl} They are all $10$ to a power of $2$, and the only
differences are [where the minus sign goes]{.hl} and whether the number is $99$ or $100$. So this is not
really a calculation. It is two questions: is $x_{100}$ bigger or smaller than $1$, and [how many square
roots have you taken by the time you get to the 100th term?]{.hl}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[Write out the first few terms]{.hl} and keep your eye on the power of $10$:

$$x_1 = 10^{1}, \qquad x_2 = 10^{1/2}, \qquad x_3 = 10^{1/4}, \qquad x_4 = 10^{1/8}, \qquad \dots$$

[Every square root halves the power]{.hl}. Going from $x_1$ to $x_n$ we halve it $n-1$ times, so

$$x_n = 10^{\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}} = 10^{\,2^{-(n-1)}} , \qquad \text{giving} \qquad x_{100} = 10^{\,2^{-99}} ,$$

which is **option C**. $\blacksquare$

Now do the two checks. If you square-root a number bigger than $1$, you get something smaller — but
still bigger than $1$. So every term stays above $1$, which means [the power of $10$ has to be
positive]{.hl}, and that [rules out E, F, G and H straight away]{.hl}. And going from term 1 to term 100
is **ninety-nine** square roots, not a hundred, which rules out B and D.

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $2^{-100}$ — off by one: a hundred halvings counted instead of ninety-nine. The most tempting wrong answer on the paper. |
| **A**, **B** | A positive power, $2^{99}$ or $2^{100}$ — as if the terms were being *squared* rather than square-rooted. |
| **E**, **F**, **G**, **H** | A minus sign in front of the $2$ — mixing up *halving* the power with *negating* it. All of these are less than $1$, but every term of this sequence is bigger than $1$. |

That last row is the easiest mark on the page to throw away. You can do the whole question perfectly,
get $10^{2^{-99}}$, and then pick option E, $10^{-2^{99}}$, because at a glance they look the same. The
minus sign goes *inside*, on the $99$. [Read the option you are about to choose, not the one you expect
to see.]{.hl}
:::

## Question 5

::: {.topic}
Topic — geometric series; a hidden quadratic under the substitution $u = r^3$
:::

::: {.question}
$S$ is a geometric sequence. The sum of the first $6$ terms of $S$ is equal to $9$ times the sum of the
first $3$ terms. The $7$th term of $S$ is $360$. Find the $1$st term of $S$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac{40}{27}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\tfrac{40}{9}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\tfrac{40}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $\tfrac{45}{16}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{45}{8}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $\tfrac{45}{4}$
:::

The first condition looks like it involves both $a$ and $r$, but it doesn't. When you write out the two
sums, [the $a$ cancels from both sides]{.hl}, and so does the $1-r$ — so [the first condition only tells
you about $r$]{.hl}, and the second one then gives you $a$. What's left has $r^6$ and $r^3$ in it, and
since $r^6 = (r^3)^2$, [it's a quadratic in disguise]{.hl}: let $u = r^3$ and it becomes an ordinary one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$, the condition $S_6 = 9S_3$ says

$$\frac{a(1-r^6)}{1-r} = 9 \cdot \frac{a(1-r^3)}{1-r} .$$

[Cancel the $a$ and the $1-r$ from both sides]{.hl}:

$$1 - r^6 = 9\left(1 - r^3\right) .$$

Now [let $u = r^3$]{.hl}, so that $r^6 = u^2$:

$$1 - u^2 = 9(1-u) , \qquad \text{that is} \qquad (1-u)(1+u) = 9(1-u) .$$

[Be careful here — don't just cancel the $(1-u)$]{.hl}. If you do, you throw away the case $u=1$ without
checking it. So deal with it first: $u=1$ means $r=1$, and if $r=1$ the sequence is just $a,a,a,\dots$,
so $S_6 = 6a$ and $S_3 = 3a$. That gives $S_6 = 2S_3$, not $9S_3$, so $r=1$ doesn't work and we can
safely divide:

$$1 + u = 9 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u = 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^3 = 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 2 .$$

The 7th term is $ar^6$ — [count the powers carefully]{.hl}, it's $r^6$, not $r^7$ — so

$$64a = 360 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a = \frac{360}{64} = \frac{45}{8} ,$$

which is **option E**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **F** | $\tfrac{45}{4} = \tfrac{360}{32}$ — used $ar^5$ for the 7th term. Off by one. |
| **D** | $\tfrac{45}{16} = \tfrac{360}{128}$ — used $ar^7$. Off by one the other way. |
| **A**, **B**, **C** | All of the form $\tfrac{360}{3^k}$, so they come from getting $r=3$ plus an index slip. No clean route gives $r=3$; these are just decoys. |

Look at the option list: three of them are $\tfrac{45}{2^k}$ and three are $\tfrac{40}{3^k}$. That is
the examiner telling you the question is *find $r$, then get the index right* — and that plenty of
people will do the first part and fall over on the second.
:::

## Question 6

::: {.topic}
Topic — circles; the distance between two centres
:::

::: {.question}
The circles with equations
$$(x+4)^2 + (y+1)^2 = 64 \qquad\text{and}\qquad (x-8)^2 + (y-4)^2 = r^2 \quad (r>0)$$
have exactly one point in common. Find the difference between the two possible values of $r$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $10$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $16$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $26$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $50$
:::

Don't touch the algebra — [draw the picture]{.hl}. Two circles meet at exactly one point when they
**touch**, and [there are two ways for circles to touch]{.hl}: side by side, or one sitting inside the
other. The question says *"the two possible values of $r$"*, which is telling you that both happen here.
Everything then comes from [the distance between the two centres]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Read the centres and the radius straight off the equations: the first circle has centre $(-4,-1)$ and
radius $\sqrt{64} = 8$; the second has centre $(8,4)$ and radius $r$.

The distance between the centres is

$$d = \sqrt{\big(8-(-4)\big)^2 + \big(4-(-1)\big)^2} = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13 .$$

[Watch the signs on those coordinates]{.hl} — it's $4 - (-1) = 5$, not $4 - 1 = 3$. And notice you get
$5, 12, 13$: a Pythagorean triple. [TMUA questions are built on triples on purpose]{.hl}, because you
have no calculator. If a root is coming out ugly, you have made a mistake.

Now the two ways of touching:

- **Touching on the outside.** The centres are $8 + r$ apart, so $8 + r = 13$ and $r = 5$.
- **One circle inside the other.** Now the big radius minus the small one is the gap between the
  centres: $r - 8 = 13$, so $r = 21$.

The difference is $21 - 5 = 16$, which is **option C**. $\blacksquare$

Here is the neat part. [The difference is $(d+8)-(d-8) = 16$, so the distance cancels]{.hl} — you never
needed to work out $d$ at all. The answer is always twice the radius you were *given*.

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $26 = 2\times 13$ — the right idea (*double it*) applied to the **distance** instead of the radius. |
| **B** | $10 = 2\times 5$ — doubled the radius they found rather than the one they were given. |
| **A**, **E** | No clear origin. |

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 10.6))
C1, C2, R1 = (-4, -1), (8, 4), 8
for ax, r, lim, title in [
        (axes[0], 5,  15, 'Touching on the outside:   $d = 8 + r$,   $r = 13 - 8 = 5$'),
        (axes[1], 21, 31, 'One inside the other:   $d = r - 8$,   $r = 13 + 8 = 21$')]:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle(C1, R1, fill=False, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2))
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle(C2, r,  fill=False, color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2))
    ax.plot(*zip(C1, C2), 'k--', lw=1.2)
    ax.plot(*C1, 'o', color=ROOT_CLR, ms=5); ax.plot(*C2, 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=5)
    if r == 5:
        tx, ty = C1[0] + 12*R1/13, C1[1] + 5*R1/13
    else:
        tx, ty = C2[0] - 12*r/13, C2[1] - 5*r/13
    box = dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.25', fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.92)
    ax.plot([tx], [ty], '*', color='k', ms=16, zorder=6)
    ax.annotate('the one\ncommon point', (tx, ty), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(14, -40),
                fontsize=9, bbox=box, zorder=7, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-', lw=0.8))
    ax.annotate('$(-4,-1)$,  $r_1=8$', C1, textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-18, -22),
                fontsize=9, color=ROOT_CLR, bbox=box, zorder=7)
    ax.annotate('$(8,4)$', C2, textcoords='offset points', xytext=(9, 6), fontsize=9,
                color=ASYM_CLR, bbox=box, zorder=7)
    ax.annotate('$d=13$', (2, 1.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-4, 14), fontsize=9,
                bbox=box, zorder=7)
    ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.grid(alpha=0.25); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(-lim-6, lim+6); ax.set_ylim(-lim-4, lim+4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 7

::: {.topic}
Topic — the product rule; minimising with respect to a second variable
:::

::: {.question}
A curve has equation $y = (2q - x^2)(2qx + 3)$. The gradient of the curve at $x = -1$ is a function of
$q$. Find the value of $q$ which minimises the gradient of the curve at $x=-1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-\tfrac34$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $-\tfrac12$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac12$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $\tfrac34$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $1$
:::

There are two letters here and [you differentiate with respect to a different one each time]{.hl}. First
differentiate with respect to $x$ to get the gradient, treating $q$ as a constant. Then put $x=-1$ in,
which leaves you with an expression in $q$ alone. Only *then* do you differentiate with respect to $q$,
to make that expression as small as possible. [Say the three stages out loud before you start]{.hl} —
the mistake this question is fishing for is doing stage one and stopping.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Stage 1 — differentiate with respect to $x$**, holding $q$ constant. Use the product rule:

$$\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} = (-2x)(2qx+3) + (2q - x^2)(2q) .$$

**Stage 2 — put $x = -1$ in**:

$$\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=-1} = (2)(-2q+3) + (2q-1)(2q) = -4q + 6 + 4q^2 - 2q = 4q^2 - 6q + 6 .$$

[Now stop and look at what you've got]{.hl}: a quadratic in $q$, with a positive coefficient of $q^2$.
So it opens upwards, which means it really does have a minimum, and the minimum is at the vertex.

**Stage 3 — differentiate with respect to $q$** and set it to zero:

$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dq}\left(4q^2 - 6q + 6\right) = 8q - 6 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q = \frac{3}{4} ,$$

which is **option F**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $q=0$ — this is what you get if you set the *gradient* equal to zero instead of **minimising** it. You have answered a different question, and it is a very easy one to drift into. |
| **B** | $-\tfrac34$ — a sign slip in the product rule, giving $4q^2 + 6q + 6$. |
| **E** | $\tfrac12$ — consistent with an arithmetic slip leaving $8q-4=0$. |
| **A**, **C**, **G** | No single clear slip. |
:::

## Question 8

::: {.topic}
Topic — the trapezium rule; graph transformations
:::

::: {.question}
The function $\mathrm f$ is such that $0 < \mathrm f(x) < 1$ for $0 \le x \le 1$. The trapezium rule with
$n$ equal intervals is used to estimate $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$ and produces an
**underestimate**. Using the same number of equal intervals, for which one of the following does the
trapezium rule produce an **overestimate**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (\mathrm f(x)+1)\,\mathrm dx$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**B** $\displaystyle\int_0^1 2\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**C** $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0 \mathrm f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0 \mathrm f(-x)\,\mathrm dx$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (1 - \mathrm f(x))\,\mathrm dx$
:::

[Don't try to picture five different graphs.]{.hl} Ask one question about each option instead: *does this
transformation change the **sign** of the error?* The trapezium rule underestimates when the curve is
concave (bending downwards) and overestimates when it is convex — so [you are looking for the option
that turns the curve upside down]{.hl}. Shifting, stretching, translating and reflecting all leave the
bend the same way up. [Only one of the five flips it]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Call the trapezium estimate of $\int_0^1 \mathrm f$ by the name $T$, and the true value $I$. We are told
$T < I$: an underestimate.

- **A.** Adding $1$ lifts the curve and the trapezia by exactly the same amount. The new estimate is
  $T+1$ and the new true value is $I+1$, so $T+1 < I+1$ — [still an underestimate]{.hl}.
- **B.** Doubling doubles both: $2T < 2I$. The error gets bigger, but [doubling a negative error keeps
  it negative]{.hl}.
- **C.** Substituting $u = x+1$ turns this into $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(u)\,\mathrm du$ — the same graph,
  just [slid sideways]{.hl}. The trapezia slide with it, so the error is identical.
- **D.** Substituting $u = -x$ also gives $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(u)\,\mathrm du$ — the graph reflected in
  the $y$-axis. The trapezia reflect too, so again the error is identical.
- **E.** Here the estimate is $1 - T$ and the true value is $1 - I$. Subtracting **flips the
  inequality**: since $T < I$, we get $1 - T > 1 - I$. So the estimate is now bigger than the true
  value — an **overestimate**.

**Option E.** $\blacksquare$

The idea underneath is simple: $1 - \mathrm f$ is the only one of the five that [turns the curve upside
down]{.hl}. A concave curve becomes convex, and the trapezium rule swaps from under to over.

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** | "The graph moved up, so the estimate must go up" — true, but the *true value* went up by exactly the same amount. |
| **B** | "The error doubled" — yes, and twice a negative number is still negative. |
| **C**, **D** | Believing that sliding or reflecting a graph changes how the trapezia sit against it. One picture kills both. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
f = 0.15 + 0.8*np.sqrt(x)          # concave, and 0 < f < 1
nodes = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.0, 8.4))

axes[0].plot(x, f, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=\mathrm{f}(x)$  (concave)')
axes[0].fill_between(nodes, 0.15 + 0.8*np.sqrt(nodes), color=ASYM_CLR, alpha=0.18,
                     label='trapezia — they fall SHORT')
axes[0].plot(nodes, 0.15 + 0.8*np.sqrt(nodes), color=ASYM_CLR, lw=1.5, marker='o', ms=4)
axes[0].set_title('The curve bends downwards: the chords lie below it → UNDERestimate', fontsize=11)

g = 1 - f                           # convex
axes[1].plot(x, g, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=1-\mathrm{f}(x)$  (convex)')
axes[1].fill_between(nodes, 1 - (0.15 + 0.8*np.sqrt(nodes)), color=ASYM_CLR, alpha=0.18,
                     label='trapezia — they OVERshoot')
axes[1].plot(nodes, 1 - (0.15 + 0.8*np.sqrt(nodes)), color=ASYM_CLR, lw=1.5, marker='o', ms=4)
axes[1].set_title('Subtracting from 1 turns it upside down: chords above → OVERestimate', fontsize=11)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
    ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='lower right'); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 9

::: {.topic}
Topic — the area between two curves
:::

::: {.question}
$p$ is a positive constant. Find the area enclosed between the curves $y = p\sqrt{x}$ and $x = p\sqrt{y}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac23 p^{5/2} - \tfrac12 p^2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\tfrac43 p^{5/2} - p^2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**C** $\tfrac{p^4}{6}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $\tfrac{p^4}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $\tfrac23 p^3 - \tfrac12 p^4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $\tfrac43 p^3 - p^4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $2p^4$
:::

The two curves are [mirror images of each other in the line $y=x$]{.hl} — swap $x$ and $y$ in one and
you get the other. Before you integrate anything, look at the options: [every term in the answer must
have the same power of $p$]{.hl}, because scaling $p$ just scales the whole picture. Four of the seven
options mix $p^{5/2}$ with $p^2$, or $p^3$ with $p^4$, so [they are impossible without any working at
all]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

First [make both curves functions of $x$]{.hl}. Square both sides of $x = p\sqrt y$:

$$x^2 = p^2 y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y = \frac{x^2}{p^2} .$$

(Squaring is safe here because $\sqrt y \ge 0$ and $p > 0$, so both sides are positive to begin with.)

Now find where they meet:

$$p\sqrt x = \frac{x^2}{p^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p^3 \sqrt x = x^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p^3 = x^{3/2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = p^2 ,$$

together with $x=0$. Between them, [the square root curve is the one on top]{.hl} — check a small value
of $x$ if you're not sure.

$$A = \int_0^{p^2}\left(p\sqrt x - \frac{x^2}{p^2}\right)\mathrm dx
   = \left[\frac{2p}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{x^3}{3p^2}\right]_0^{p^2}
   = \frac{2p}{3}\cdot p^3 - \frac{p^6}{3p^2}
   = \frac{2p^4}{3} - \frac{p^4}{3} = \frac{p^4}{3} ,$$

which is **option D**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **C** | $\tfrac{p^4}{6}$ — halved once too often, or only one of the two curves integrated. |
| **G** | $2p^4$ — a factor-of-six slip on the same integral. |
| **A**, **B**, **E**, **F** | **Impossible on sight** — they mix powers of $p$. They come from squaring or rooting one term but not the other. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

p = 2.0
xs = np.linspace(0, p**2, 400)
upper, lower = p*np.sqrt(xs), xs**2/p**2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.6))
ax.plot(xs, upper, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=p\sqrt{x}$')
ax.plot(xs, lower, color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$x=p\sqrt{y}\;\Leftrightarrow\;y=x^2/p^2$')
ax.fill_between(xs, lower, upper, color=ROOT_CLR, alpha=0.15)
ax.plot(xs, xs, 'k:', lw=1, label='$y=x$  — the curves are mirror images in this line')
for X, Y in [(0, 0), (p**2, p**2)]:
    ax.plot([X], [Y], 'o', color=YINT_CLR, ms=7, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'they meet at $(p^2,\,p^2)$', (p**2, p**2), textcoords='offset points',
            xytext=(-104, 8), color=YINT_CLR, fontsize=10)
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.set_title(r'Shaded area $= p^4/3$   (drawn with $p=2$)')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 10

::: {.topic}
Topic — integrating a function containing a modulus
:::

::: {.question}
Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{3} |x|(1-x)\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac{17}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-\tfrac{17}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\tfrac{16}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $-\tfrac{16}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{11}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $-\tfrac{11}{3}$
:::

[You can't integrate $|x|$ in one go]{.hl}, because it isn't one function — it's two, glued together at
$x=0$. On the left of zero it is $-x$; on the right it is $x$. So [split the integral where the modulus
changes]{.hl}, and do two integrals. One more thing before you start: the region from $0$ to $3$ is wide
and mostly *below* the axis, so [you should expect a negative answer]{.hl} — which already kills three of
the six options.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Split at $x = 0$.

On $-1 \le x \le 0$ we have $|x| = -x$, so the integrand is $-x(1-x) = -x + x^2$:

$$\int_{-1}^{0}\left(-x + x^2\right)\mathrm dx = \left[-\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}
= 0 - \left(-\frac12 - \frac13\right) = \frac56 .$$

On $0 \le x \le 3$ we have $|x| = x$, so the integrand is $x - x^2$:

$$\int_{0}^{3}\left(x - x^2\right)\mathrm dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3}
= \frac92 - 9 = -\frac92 .$$

[Add the two pieces together]{.hl}:

$$\frac56 - \frac92 = \frac{5}{6} - \frac{27}{6} = -\frac{22}{6} = -\frac{11}{3} ,$$

which is **option F**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $-\tfrac{16}{3}$ — this is exactly what you get if you **ignore the modulus completely** and integrate $x(1-x)$ from $-1$ to $3$ in one go. That is why it is on the list. |
| **C** | $+\tfrac{16}{3}$ — the same omission, plus a sign error. |
| **E** | $+\tfrac{11}{3}$ — all the work correct, then the sign dropped at the last line. |
| **A**, **B** | $\pm\tfrac{17}{3}$ — no clear origin. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

x1 = np.linspace(-1, 0, 200); y1 = -x1*(1 - x1)
x2 = np.linspace(0, 3, 300);  y2 =  x2*(1 - x2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 4.8))
ax.plot(x1, y1, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2)
ax.plot(x2, y2, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=|x|(1-x)$')
ax.fill_between(x1, y1, color=YINT_CLR, alpha=0.25, label=r'$x<0$:  area $=+\frac{5}{6}$')
ax.fill_between(x2, y2, color=ASYM_CLR, alpha=0.20, label=r'$x>0$:  area $=-\frac{9}{2}$')
ax.axvline(0, color='k', ls='--', lw=1.2)
ax.text(0.06, -3.6, 'split here —\nthe modulus\nchanges at $x=0$', fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.9)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.set_title('The negative region is much bigger, so the answer must be negative')
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='lower left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 11

::: {.topic}
Topic — laws of logarithms; simultaneous equations; a hidden quadratic
:::

::: {.question}
Find the sum of the real values of $x$ that satisfy the simultaneous equations
$$\log_3(xy^2) = 1 , \qquad (\log_3 x)(\log_3 y) = -3 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac13$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $3\tfrac19$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $9\tfrac1{27}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $9\tfrac13$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $27$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $27\tfrac19$
:::

These equations are not really about $x$ and $y$ — [they are about $\log_3 x$ and $\log_3 y$]{.hl}. So
[give those two things names]{.hl}, say $a$ and $b$, split the first log using the log laws, and you are
left with two ordinary simultaneous equations. Two warnings. The question asks for the sum of the values
of **$x$**, not of $a$ — so [remember to convert back at the end]{.hl}. And look at the options: five of
them are *a power of 3 plus a smaller power of 3*, which tells you what shape the answer will take.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Let $a = \log_3 x$ and $b = \log_3 y$.

Split the first equation using the log laws — [a product becomes a sum, and a power comes down to the
front]{.hl}:

$$\log_3(xy^2) = \log_3 x + 2\log_3 y = a + 2b = 1 .$$

The second equation is simply $ab = -3$. So we have

$$a + 2b = 1 , \qquad ab = -3 .$$

[Substitute $a = 1 - 2b$ into the second one]{.hl}:

$$(1-2b)b = -3 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2b^2 - b - 3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (2b-3)(b+1) = 0 ,$$

so $b = \tfrac32$ or $b = -1$.

Now convert back. Since $a = \log_3 x$, we have $x = 3^a$:

- $b = \tfrac32 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 1 - 3 = -2 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 3^{-2} = \tfrac19$
- $b = -1 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 1 + 2 = 3 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 3^{3} = 27$

Both are fine — $x$ and $y$ both come out positive, which they have to for the logs to exist in the
first place. The sum is

$$27 + \tfrac19 = 27\tfrac19 ,$$

which is **option H**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **G** | $27$ — found both roots, then gave **only one $x$** instead of the sum. Read the first line of the question again. |
| **D**, **E**, **F** | The right shape ($3^{a_1} + 3^{a_2}$), the wrong pair of roots — a slip in solving the quadratic. |
| **A**, **B**, **C** | Small values — consistent with solving for $y$, or with quoting $a$ and $b$ instead of $x$. |
:::

## Question 12

::: {.topic}
Topic — integration after simplifying; the difference of two squares
:::

::: {.question}
It is given that
$$\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{24\pi(t-1)}{1+\sqrt t} \quad \text{for } t \ge 1 ,$$
and $V = 7$ when $t = 1$. Find the value of $V$ when $t = 9$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $208\pi+7$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $216\pi+7$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $224\pi+7$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $416\pi+7$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $608\pi+7$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $744\pi+7$
:::

Your instinct will be to reach for a substitution — [don't]{.hl}. Look at the fraction for five seconds
first. The top is $t-1$, and $t$ is $(\sqrt t)^2$, so [$t-1$ is a difference of two squares in
disguise]{.hl}. Factorise it and the bottom cancels straight out, leaving an integral you can do in your
head. That cancellation is not luck: [when something in a TMUA question looks ugly, the ugliness is
usually about to disappear]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Write $t = \left(\sqrt t\right)^2$, so that

$$t - 1 = \left(\sqrt t\right)^2 - 1^2 = \left(\sqrt t - 1\right)\left(\sqrt t + 1\right) .$$

The $\left(\sqrt t + 1\right)$ [cancels with the denominator]{.hl}, leaving

$$\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dt} = 24\pi\left(\sqrt t - 1\right) = 24\pi\left(t^{1/2} - 1\right) .$$

Now integrate:

$$V = 24\pi\left(\frac{2}{3}t^{3/2} - t\right) + C .$$

Use the condition $V = 7$ at $t=1$ to find $C$:

$$7 = 24\pi\left(\tfrac23 - 1\right) + C = -8\pi + C \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C = 7 + 8\pi .$$

[Don't lose that $8\pi$]{.hl} — it is the whole difference between the right answer and option B. Finally,
at $t=9$ we have $t^{3/2} = 27$, so

$$V = 24\pi\left(\tfrac23 \times 27 - 9\right) + 7 + 8\pi = 24\pi(18-9) + 7 + 8\pi = 216\pi + 8\pi + 7 = 224\pi + 7 ,$$

which is **option C**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **B** | $216\pi + 7$ — evaluated the antiderivative at $t=9$ and **forgot the lower limit**, dropping the $8\pi$ that came from $t=1$. |
| **A** | $208\pi + 7$ — the $8\pi$ included, but subtracted instead of added. |
| **D**, **E**, **F** | No clear origin; consistent with failing to cancel and then mis-integrating the fraction. |
:::

## Question 13

::: {.topic}
Topic — a hidden quadratic; the range of the substituted variable
:::

::: {.question}
Find the maximum value of $\;4^{\sin x} - 4 \times 2^{\sin x} + \dfrac{17}{4}\;$ for real $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac14$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\tfrac52$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\tfrac{13}{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $\tfrac{21}{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{65}{4}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** There is no maximum value.
:::

There isn't a single $x^2$ in sight, but [$4^{\sin x} = \left(2^{\sin x}\right)^2$]{.hl} — so the
expression is built out of $2^{\sin x}$ and its square, and it is a quadratic after all. Let $u =
2^{\sin x}$. Then comes the step that decides this question: [$u$ is not free to be anything]{.hl}.
Since $\sin x$ can only run between $-1$ and $1$, [$u$ is trapped in a closed interval]{.hl} — and
option F is sitting there waiting for anyone who forgets it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Let $u = 2^{\sin x}$. Then $4^{\sin x} = \left(2^2\right)^{\sin x} = \left(2^{\sin x}\right)^2 = u^2$,
so the expression becomes

$$u^2 - 4u + \tfrac{17}{4} .$$

Now [work out the range of $u$]{.hl}. Since $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$,

$$2^{-1} \le u \le 2^{1} , \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \tfrac12 \le u \le 2 .$$

Complete the square:

$$u^2 - 4u + \tfrac{17}{4} = (u-2)^2 + \tfrac14 .$$

[Be careful — the vertex is a MINIMUM here]{.hl}, not a maximum, because the parabola opens upwards.
On a closed interval, [the maximum of an upward parabola is at one of the endpoints]{.hl}, and it is the
endpoint furthest from the vertex that wins. Test them:

$$u = 2: \quad (2-2)^2 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac14 \qquad\text{(the minimum)}$$
$$u = \tfrac12: \quad \left(\tfrac12 - 2\right)^2 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac94 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac{10}{4} = \tfrac52 \qquad\checkmark$$

So the maximum is $\tfrac52$, reached when $2^{\sin x} = \tfrac12$, i.e. when $\sin x = -1$. That is
**option B**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **F** | "There is no maximum" — exactly what you conclude if you **forget that $u$ is bounded**. Let $u$ run free and $u^2 - 4u + \tfrac{17}{4} \to \infty$. This is the most instructive wrong answer on the paper. |
| **A** | $\tfrac14$ — found the vertex and quoted it: gave the **minimum** when asked for the maximum. |
| **C**, **D**, **E** | Endpoint values from a wrong range for $u$ — for instance taking $u \in [-1,1]$, or substituting $u = 4^{\sin x}$. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

u = np.linspace(-0.4, 3.4, 400)
y = u**2 - 4*u + 17/4

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 5.0))
ax.plot(u, y, color='#999', lw=1.6, ls='--', label=r'$u^2-4u+\frac{17}{4}$  (if $u$ were free)')
uu = np.linspace(0.5, 2, 200)
ax.plot(uu, uu**2 - 4*uu + 17/4, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=3,
        label=r'the part that actually exists:  $\frac{1}{2}\leq u\leq 2$')
ax.axvspan(0.5, 2, color=ROOT_CLR, alpha=0.07)

ax.plot([0.5], [0.5**2 - 4*0.5 + 17/4], 'o', color=YINT_CLR, ms=10, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'MAXIMUM $=\frac{5}{2}$' '\n' r'at the endpoint $u=\frac{1}{2}$',
            (0.5, 2.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(16, 6), fontsize=10, color=YINT_CLR)
ax.plot([2], [0.25], 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=9, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'vertex is the MINIMUM $=\frac{1}{4}$', (2, 0.25), textcoords='offset points',
            xytext=(10, -6), fontsize=10, color=ASYM_CLR)

for c in (0.5, 2):
    ax.axvline(c, color=ROOT_CLR, ls=':', lw=1.2)
ax.set_xlabel(r'$u = 2^{\sin x}$'); ax.set_ylabel('value')
ax.set_title(r'$u$ is trapped in $[\frac{1}{2},\,2]$ — so the maximum is at an endpoint, not at the vertex')
ax.grid(alpha=0.25); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper center')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 14

::: {.topic}
Topic — solving two linear equations in $\sin 2x$ and $\cos 2x$; the doubled range
:::

::: {.question}
$x$ satisfies the simultaneous equations
$$\sin 2x + \sqrt3 \cos 2x = -1 , \qquad \sqrt3 \sin 2x - \cos 2x = \sqrt3 ,$$
where $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$. Find the sum of the possible values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $210^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $330^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $390^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $660^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $780^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $930^\circ$
:::

[These are not two trig equations — they are two *linear* equations]{.hl}, in the two unknowns
$\sin 2x$ and $\cos 2x$. So call them $s$ and $c$ and solve the pair like any other simultaneous
equations; only afterwards do you think about angles. Then the trap: the range is on $x$, but you are
solving for $2x$, so [write down the range for $2x$ before you go looking]{.hl} — it runs from $0^\circ$
to $720^\circ$, which is **two** full turns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Put $s = \sin 2x$ and $c = \cos 2x$:

$$s + \sqrt3\,c = -1 , \qquad \sqrt3\,s - c = \sqrt3 .$$

From the second equation, $c = \sqrt3 s - \sqrt3$. [Substitute that into the first]{.hl}:

$$s + \sqrt3\left(\sqrt3 s - \sqrt3\right) = -1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad s + 3s - 3 = -1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 4s = 2 ,$$

so $s = \tfrac12$, and then $c = \sqrt3 \cdot \tfrac12 - \sqrt3 = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

[Sanity check: $s^2 + c^2 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac34 = 1$]{.hl}, as it must be. If it doesn't come to $1$, you
have made an arithmetic mistake and there is no point going on.

So we need $\sin 2x = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 2x = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ **at the same time**. Sine positive,
cosine negative puts $2x$ in the second quadrant, and the angle is

$$2x = 150^\circ \quad (+\, 360^\circ k) .$$

Now use the range. Since $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, we have $0^\circ \le 2x \le 720^\circ$, so there
are **two** solutions, not one:

$$2x = 150^\circ \text{ or } 510^\circ \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 75^\circ \text{ or } 255^\circ .$$

The sum is $75 + 255 = 330^\circ$, which is **option B**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $660^\circ = 150 + 510$ — added up the values of **$2x$** and forgot to halve. Far and away the most likely slip. |
| **A**, **C**, **E**, **F** | No clear origin; consistent with solving only one of the two equations and picking up extra solutions. |

The reason the question uses $\sin 2x$ rather than $\sin x$ is precisely to create the $720^\circ$ trap.
[Whenever you see $\sin 2x$ with a range given on $x$, write the range for $2x$ on your paper first]{.hl}.
:::

## Question 15

::: {.topic}
Topic — indices with the same base; a hidden quadratic
:::

::: {.question}
Find the real **non-zero** solution to the equation
$$\frac{2^{(9^x)}}{8^{(3^x)}} = \frac14 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\log_3 2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $2\log_3 2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\log_2 3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $2\log_2 3$
:::

Everything in sight is a power of $2$ or a power of $3$, so [get every base the same and then compare the
exponents]{.hl}. Once you do, what is left has $9^x$ and $3^x$ in it — and $9^x = \left(3^x\right)^2$, so
[it's another hidden quadratic]{.hl}. One more thing: the question says *non-zero*, and [a question only
says that when zero is a solution]{.hl}. That is a free hint about what is coming.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Write $8$ and $\tfrac14$ as powers of $2$:

$$8^{\left(3^x\right)} = \left(2^3\right)^{\left(3^x\right)} = 2^{\,3\cdot 3^x} , \qquad \frac14 = 2^{-2} .$$

So the equation becomes

$$\frac{2^{\left(9^x\right)}}{2^{\,3\cdot 3^x}} = 2^{-2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2^{\,9^x - 3\cdot 3^x} = 2^{-2} .$$

[Same base, so we can compare the powers]{.hl}:

$$9^x - 3\cdot 3^x = -2 .$$

Now [let $y = 3^x$]{.hl}, so that $9^x = \left(3^x\right)^2 = y^2$:

$$y^2 - 3y + 2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y-1)(y-2) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y = 1 \text{ or } y = 2 .$$

[Substitute back — $y$ was our invention, not the answer]{.hl}:

- $y = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; 3^x = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 0$. But the question asked for the **non-zero**
  solution, so this one is ruled out — and now you see why the word was there.
- $y = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; 3^x = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \log_3 2$. ✓

So the answer is $\log_3 2$, which is **option A**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** | $2$ — solved the quadratic and gave **$y$** instead of $x$. Forgot to substitute back. |
| **E**, **F** | $\log_2 3$ and $2\log_2 3$ — the **base is upside down**. From $3^x = 2$ you get $x = \log_3 2$, not $\log_2 3$. Quick check: $\log_3 2 < 1$ because $2 < 3$, whereas $\log_2 3 > 1$. |
| **C** | $1$ — from mis-solving $3^x = 1$. |
| **B** | $2\log_3 2 = \log_3 4$ — from $y=4$, or from doubling the right answer. |
:::

## Question 16

::: {.topic}
Topic — definite integrals; a translation does not change the area
:::

::: {.question}
Given that
$$2\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx + 5\int_1^2 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx = 14 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_0^1 \mathrm f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx = 6 ,$$
find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-8$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $-2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $\tfrac{29}{5}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $\tfrac{32}{5}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $14$
:::

The whole question turns on one thing, and it is hiding in the second piece of information.
[$\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx$ is **not** $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$]{.hl} — the $x+1$
shifts the graph sideways. Substitute $u = x+1$ and the limits move with it. In plain English: [sliding a
graph sideways doesn't change the area underneath it]{.hl}; it only changes the labels on the axis. Miss
that, and you will get a perfectly clean wrong answer that is sitting on the option list.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Deal with the second equation first. [Let $u = x + 1$]{.hl}. When $x = 0$, $u = 1$; when $x=1$, $u=2$;
and $\mathrm du = \mathrm dx$. So

$$\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx = \int_1^2 \mathrm f(u)\,\mathrm du = 6 .$$

So we have actually been told the value of $\int_1^2 \mathrm f$, not $\int_0^1 \mathrm f$.

Now write $P = \int_0^1 \mathrm f$ and $Q = \int_1^2 \mathrm f$. We know $Q = 6$, so from the first
equation

$$2P + 5(6) = 14 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2P = -16 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P = -8 .$$

[$P$ comes out negative, and that is perfectly fine]{.hl} — nobody said $\mathrm f$ was positive, and a
definite integral is a *signed* area. Finally,

$$\int_0^2 \mathrm f = P + Q = -8 + 6 = -2 ,$$

which is **option C**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **G** | $\tfrac{32}{5}$ — read $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x+1)\,\mathrm dx$ as $\int_0^1 \mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$, i.e. **missed the translation**. Then $P = 6$, $Q = \tfrac25$, and $P + Q = \tfrac{32}{5}$ exactly. This is the trap the question was built around. |
| **A** | $-8$ — that is $P$: **stopped one step early** and gave $\int_0^1$ instead of $\int_0^2$. |
| **H** | $14$ — a number copied straight from the question. |
| **B**, **D**, **E**, **F** | No clear origin. |
:::

## Question 17

::: {.topic}
Topic — a product of two factors; sign tables
:::

::: {.question}
Find the fraction of the interval $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for which
$$\Big(\sin 2\theta - \tfrac12\Big)\Big(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\Big) \ge 0 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac1{12}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\tfrac16$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\tfrac14$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $\tfrac5{12}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac7{12}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $\tfrac34$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** $\tfrac56$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** $\tfrac{11}{12}$
:::

Whatever you do, [don't expand the brackets]{.hl}. A product of two things is $\ge 0$ exactly when [the
two factors have the same sign]{.hl} (or one of them is zero). So find where each factor is zero, mark
those points on the interval, and [build a sign table]{.hl}. One hint from the examiner: every option is
a number of twelfths, which is telling you how the interval is going to be cut up.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**First factor.** $\sin 2\theta - \tfrac12 = 0$ means $\sin 2\theta = \tfrac12$, so
$2\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$ or $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$, giving

$$\theta = \frac{\pi}{12} \quad\text{or}\quad \theta = \frac{5\pi}{12} .$$

[Careful: it's $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, not $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$]{.hl} — $\sin$ is $\tfrac12$ at $30^\circ$, and
$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ at $60^\circ$. From the sine graph, $\sin 2\theta$ is *above* $\tfrac12$ between
these two values, and below it elsewhere on $[0,\pi]$.

**Second factor.** $\sin\theta = \cos\theta$ means $\tan\theta = 1$, so $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Below
that, cosine is the bigger of the two, so the factor is negative; above it, positive.

Write all three critical values in twelfths: $\tfrac{\pi}{12}$, $\tfrac{3\pi}{12}$, $\tfrac{5\pi}{12}$.
Now the sign table:

| $\theta$ | $0 \to \tfrac{\pi}{12}$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{12} \to \tfrac{3\pi}{12}$ | $\tfrac{3\pi}{12} \to \tfrac{5\pi}{12}$ | $\tfrac{5\pi}{12} \to \pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin 2\theta - \tfrac12$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ |
| $\sin\theta - \cos\theta$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| **product** | $\mathbf{+}$ | $-$ | $\mathbf{+}$ | $-$ |

The product is $\ge 0$ on $\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{12}\right]$ and $\left[\tfrac{3\pi}{12}, \tfrac{5\pi}{12}\right]$.
[Add up the lengths]{.hl}:

$$\frac{\pi}{12} + \frac{2\pi}{12} = \frac{3\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{4} .$$

The whole interval has length $\pi$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{\pi/4}{\pi} = \dfrac14$, which is
**option C**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** | $\tfrac1{12}$ — found only the **first** of the two intervals. |
| **B** | $\tfrac16 = \tfrac2{12}$ — found only the **second**. |
| **F** | $\tfrac34$ — the **complement**: solved for where the product is $\le 0$ instead. |
| **G**, **H** | The complements of B and A — the same two errors, plus the complement error. |
| **D**, **E** | $\tfrac5{12}$, $\tfrac7{12}$ — a sign error in one row of the table. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

th = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 800)
f1, f2 = np.sin(2*th) - 0.5, np.sin(th) - np.cos(th)
prod = f1 * f2

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.4, 7.8), sharex=True)

axes[0].plot(th, f1, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$\sin 2\theta - \frac{1}{2}$')
axes[0].plot(th, f2, color=YINT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$\sin\theta - \cos\theta$')
axes[0].axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.9)
axes[0].set_title('Where does each factor change sign?', fontsize=11)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9); axes[0].grid(alpha=0.25)

axes[1].plot(th, prod, color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2, label='the product')
axes[1].axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.9)
axes[1].fill_between(th, 0, prod, where=(prod >= 0), color=ASYM_CLR, alpha=0.18,
                     label=r'product $\geq 0$:  total length $\pi/4$')
axes[1].set_title(r'The two shaded pieces make $\frac{\pi}{12}+\frac{2\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ — a quarter of the interval',
                  fontsize=11)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9); axes[1].grid(alpha=0.25)

for ax in axes:
    for c in (np.pi/12, np.pi/4, 5*np.pi/12):
        ax.axvline(c, color='grey', ls='--', lw=1)
    ax.set_xticks([0, np.pi/12, np.pi/4, 5*np.pi/12, np.pi/2, np.pi])
    ax.set_xticklabels(['$0$', r'$\frac{\pi}{12}$', r'$\frac{3\pi}{12}$', r'$\frac{5\pi}{12}$',
                        r'$\frac{\pi}{2}$', r'$\pi$'])
axes[1].set_xlabel(r'$\theta$')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 18

::: {.topic}
Topic — shortest distance from a curve to a line
:::

::: {.question}
Find the shortest distance between the curve $y = x^2 + 4$ and the line $y = 2x - 2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\sqrt5$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\tfrac{6\sqrt5}{5}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\tfrac{5\sqrt5}{3}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $5$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $6$
:::

The closest point on the curve is [the point where the tangent is parallel to the line]{.hl} — anywhere
else, you could slide along the curve and get a bit closer. So [set the derivative equal to the gradient
of the line]{.hl}, find that point, and then use the perpendicular distance formula. Two things people
get wrong: the closest point is *not* the vertex of the parabola, and [the distance is measured
perpendicular to the line, not vertically]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

First check they don't actually meet: $x^2 + 4 = 2x - 2$ gives $x^2 - 2x + 6 = 0$, whose discriminant is
$4 - 24 = -20 < 0$. No real roots, so the curve and the line never cross and the shortest distance is a
genuine positive number.

Now [find where the tangent is parallel to the line]{.hl}. The line has gradient $2$, so

$$\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} = 2x = 2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{the closest point is } (1,\,5) .$$

For the perpendicular distance formula you need the line in the form $ax + by + c = 0$, so [rewrite
$y = 2x-2$ as $2x - y - 2 = 0$]{.hl}. Then

$$d = \frac{\left|ax_0 + by_0 + c\right|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}} = \frac{\left|2(1) - (5) - 2\right|}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2}} = \frac{\left|-5\right|}{\sqrt5} = \frac{5}{\sqrt5} = \sqrt5 ,$$

which is **option B**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **F** | $5$ — the **vertical** gap between the curve and the line at $x=1$ ($5 - 0 = 5$). Measured straight down instead of perpendicular: the division by $\sqrt5$ was forgotten. |
| **C** | $\tfrac{6\sqrt5}{5} = \tfrac{6}{\sqrt5}$ — the perpendicular distance from the **vertex** $(0,4)$ instead of from the tangent point. A very natural wrong instinct: *"surely the closest point is the bottom of the curve"*. |
| **A**, **D**, **E**, **G** | No clear origin. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

xs = np.linspace(-1.0, 3.6, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 5.4))
ax.plot(xs, xs**2 + 4, color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=x^2+4$')
ax.plot(xs, 2*xs - 2,  color=ASYM_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$y=2x-2$')
ax.plot(xs, 2*xs + 3, color=YINT_CLR, ls='--', lw=1.5,
        label=r'tangent at $(1,5)$ — same gradient, $2$')

px, py = 1.0, 5.0
ax.plot([px], [py], 'o', color=YINT_CLR, ms=9, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('$(1,5)$', (px, py), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(8, 4),
            color=YINT_CLR, fontsize=10)
fx = px - 2*(2*px - py - 2)/5
fy = py + 1*(2*px - py - 2)/5
ax.plot([px, fx], [py, fy], color='k', lw=1.8)
ax.plot([fx], [fy], 'o', color='k', ms=5)
ax.annotate(r'shortest distance $=\sqrt{5}$', ((px+fx)/2, (py+fy)/2),
            textcoords='offset points', xytext=(14, -4), fontsize=10)
ax.plot([0], [4], 'o', color='#999', ms=7)
ax.annotate('the vertex —\nNOT the closest point', (0, 4), textcoords='offset points',
            xytext=(-30, 22), fontsize=9, color='#666')

ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='k', lw=0.8)
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.set_xlim(-1.0, 3.6); ax.set_ylim(-3, 10)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.set_title('Closest where the tangent is parallel to the line')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 19

::: {.topic}
Topic — a long sum whose terms repeat
:::

::: {.question}
Find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{90} \sin(10 + 90k)^\circ$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $\sin 10^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $\sin 100^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $\sin 190^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $\sin 280^\circ$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $1$
:::

Nobody is expecting you to add up ninety-one terms. So [ask what the terms *do*]{.hl} instead of what
they are. Adding $90^\circ$ four times takes you all the way round, so [the terms repeat every four
steps]{.hl} — and one full cycle adds up to nothing. Then the only real work is counting: [how many
complete cycles are there, and what is left over?]{.hl} Be careful — $k=0$ to $k=90$ is ninety-**one**
terms, not ninety.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Write out the first few terms:

$$\sin 10^\circ , \quad \sin 100^\circ , \quad \sin 190^\circ , \quad \sin 280^\circ , \quad \sin 370^\circ = \sin 10^\circ , \quad \dots$$

so the terms [repeat with period 4]{.hl}. And one complete cycle sums to zero, because

$$\sin 190^\circ = \sin(180^\circ + 10^\circ) = -\sin 10^\circ , \qquad \sin 280^\circ = -\sin 100^\circ ,$$

so

$$\sin 10^\circ + \sin 100^\circ + \sin 190^\circ + \sin 280^\circ = \sin 10^\circ + \sin 100^\circ - \sin 10^\circ - \sin 100^\circ = 0 .$$

Now count. From $k=0$ to $k=90$ inclusive there are **91** terms, and

$$91 = 4 \times 22 + 3 .$$

The 22 complete cycles (88 terms) [contribute nothing at all]{.hl}. The three left over are the first
three of a fresh cycle:

$$\sin 10^\circ + \sin 100^\circ + \sin 190^\circ = \sin 10^\circ + \sin 100^\circ - \sin 10^\circ = \sin 100^\circ .$$

So the answer is $\sin 100^\circ$, which is **option C**. $\blacksquare$

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** | $0$ — assumed everything cancels: either miscounted 91 as a multiple of 4, or forgot the leftover terms. |
| **B** | $\sin 10^\circ$ — kept only **one** leftover term instead of three. |
| **D**, **E** | Picked the wrong leftover term. |
| **F** | $1$ — no clear origin. |
:::

## Question 20

::: {.topic}
Topic — separating the constant; reading roots off a cubic
:::

::: {.question}
What is the complete range of values of $k$ for which the curves
$$y = x^3 - 12x \qquad\text{and}\qquad y = k - (x-2)^2$$
intersect at three distinct points, of which exactly two have positive $x$-coordinates?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-4<k<0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-4<k<4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $-4<k<16$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** $-16<k<0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $-16<k<4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** $-16<k<16$
:::

Set the two curves equal, and then [get all the $k$ on one side and none on the other]{.hl}. Once you do
that, the question stops being about two moving curves: it becomes [one fixed cubic and a horizontal line
$y=k$]{.hl} that you slide up and down. And *that* question is answered by a sketch — [all you need are
the turning points]{.hl}, because the number of crossings only changes when the line passes through one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Set them equal and collect the $k$:

$$x^3 - 12x = k - (x-2)^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x^3 - 12x + x^2 - 4x + 4 = k ,$$

so with $g(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 16x + 4$ the question becomes: *for which $k$ does $y = k$ cross $y = g(x)$
three times, with exactly two crossings at positive $x$?*

**Turning points.**

$$g'(x) = 3x^2 + 2x - 16 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (3x+8)(x-2) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = -\tfrac83 \text{ or } x = 2 ,$$

and

$$g\!\left(-\tfrac83\right) = \tfrac{940}{27} \approx 34.8 \quad (\text{local max}) , \qquad g(2) = -16 \quad (\text{local min}) .$$

**Condition 1 — three crossings.** A horizontal line cuts a cubic three times exactly when [it lies
between the local maximum and the local minimum]{.hl}:

$$-16 < k < \tfrac{940}{27} .$$

**Condition 2 — exactly two positive roots.** Look at the sketch. The left-hand root is always to the
left of $x = -\tfrac83$, so it is always negative; the right-hand root is always to the right of $x=2$,
so it is always positive. [So the whole condition is about the MIDDLE root]{.hl}.

On the middle branch $g$ is decreasing, and $g(0) = 4$. So the middle root is positive exactly when the
line sits **below** the height $g(0)$:

$$k < 4 .$$

Putting the two conditions together — and noting that $4 < \tfrac{940}{27}$, so this is the binding one —

$$-16 < k < 4 ,$$

which is **option E**. $\blacksquare$

Notice how cheap the second condition became once $k$ was on its own: it cost one substitution, $g(0)=4$.
Anyone who tries to keep both original curves and argue about "positive $x$-coordinates of
intersections" will not finish this in seventy-five minutes, let alone four.

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **F** | $-16<k<16$ — got the three-root condition, then never really used the second one; the upper bound is invented. |
| **D** | $-16<k<0$ — assumed "middle root positive means $k<0$", i.e. forgot to work out $g(0)$ and just used the origin. |
| **A**, **B**, **C** | All use $-4$ as the lower bound — an arithmetic slip evaluating $g(2)$, getting $-4$ instead of $-16$. |

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

g = lambda x: x**3 + x**2 - 16*x + 4
xs = np.linspace(-5.2, 4.4, 600)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 5.4))
ax.plot(xs, g(xs), color=ROOT_CLR, lw=2, label=r'$g(x)=x^3+x^2-16x+4$')

for xt, lab, off in [(-8/3, 'local max\n$g(-8/3)\\approx 34.8$', (8, -36)),
                     (2, 'local min\n$g(2)=-16$', (10, 4))]:
    ax.plot([xt], [g(xt)], 'o', color=ROOT_CLR, ms=7)
    ax.annotate(lab, (xt, g(xt)), textcoords='offset points', xytext=off, fontsize=9)

ax.axhline(-16, color=ASYM_CLR, ls='--', lw=1.5)
ax.axhline(4,   color=ASYM_CLR, ls='--', lw=1.5)
ax.text(-5.1, -14.3, r'$k=-16$', color=ASYM_CLR, fontsize=10)
ax.text(-5.1,   5.4, r'$k=4$',   color=ASYM_CLR, fontsize=10)
ax.axhspan(-16, 4, color=ASYM_CLR, alpha=0.07)

ax.plot([0], [4], 'o', color=YINT_CLR, ms=8, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'$g(0)=4$ — the middle root is positive' '\n' r'only while the line is below this',
            (0, 4), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(12, -30), color=YINT_CLR, fontsize=9)

ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='k', lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.set_title('Slide the line $y=k$: three crossings, exactly two with $x>0$, precisely when $-16<k<4$')
ax.legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
